Doma Publishing's Wizard of Oz collection has taken me several years to read with my son at bedtime. It was interesting revisiting the texts that I read swiftly through my youth, as I was about his age when I read them and remembered little beyond some of the characters that don't appear in any of the books. I picked up a copy of this version since, for 99c, I could have the complete series along with "All the original artwork by the great illustrator W.W. Denslow (over 1,000 classic illustrations)", and to read the complete 14-book text at bedtime with all original color illustrations on my Kindle Fire knowing that there would be cross-linked tables of contents and no layout issues, it was worth my buck rather than taking them all out of the library. We read these books before bed at home and under the stars by a campfire in the forest, in a hotel in Montreal and in a seaside cottage in Nova Scotia, on a boat and in a car. We read it everywhere, thanks to the Kindle's mobility. 
 You may be reading this review on one of the individual pages for the original books on Goodreads or Amazon, and if so, all I did was cross-link the books along with the correct dates we read the original texts. The only book I did not cross-link with original dates was the Woggle-bug book, which if you know, is short. Instead, I counted that final book as the review for Doma's Kindle version. You may notice that some books have longer reading spans - probably for two reasons. One, I traded off reading with my wife sometimes, and two, sometimes we needed a little Baum break and read some other books. It did get a little old sometimes, and there are fourteen books totaling 3500 pages in their original library printing. 
 The first thing I think is worth mentioning is that when I first read these books, it was as a child would read them. I remember them being repetitive but familiar. Comforting and revealing. An antiquated adventure, but a serial adventure with recurring characters unparalleled in any other literature. As an adult with an MA in literature (and soon and MFA in fiction), I am actually somewhat unimpressed with the series. Baum wrote a whimsical set of tales, but they are torturously repetitive and would be easy to plug-and-play by replacing characters and moments with a computer to make an entirely new book. But, they are children's books, and we are completely enthralled and comforted by the familiar. Is not Shakespeare the same play-to-play structurally? Are not Pixar or Star Wars movies definitively archetypal in timing, execution, structure, and character so that they can be completely replaced and reapplied to a new story? Even the films - heck, even the trailers - are cut the same, and if you play them all at once, magic happens (see: youtube, "all star wars movies at once"). 
 I suppose where the real magic of these books happens is in their origin. Baum wrote something completely original that took the world by storm and continues to be a whimsical American bellwether for children's fantasy. It is one of the original series specifically for children, spanning fourteen books written almost yearly and gobbled up by a hungry public. It still remains at the forefront of American culture in many revisits in Hollywood (let no one forget the horrific beauty that is Return To Oz) and capitalizing on nostalgia (as recently as six months ago I received a mailing from The Bradford Exchange that was selling original library-bound volumes signed by - get this - Baum's great-grandson... I love an autographed book if only for the idea of the magic it transmits even though it is somewhat meaningless, but maybe someone can convince me where the magic is in having it signed by a probably elderly great-grandchild who likely never met his great-grandfather?). 
 So, while some of the books were awesome and some of them were difficult to slog through, I have my favorites. I will also say that the introductions that each volume opens with were sweet letters from the author to his fans, and it was easy to tell that he truly, truly loved his job writing for children. He knew his audience, he knew what worked, and he sold books. Furthermore, I imagined with great sentimentality mailbags upon mailbags arriving at his house filled to the brim of letters from children all over the world, and the responsibility he probably felt to personally respond to each of them. For my career, that is the best anyone can hope for. 
 What follows is my (and my son's) short reviews of the individual books in the series. 
 The Original and Official Oz Books by L. Frank Baum 
 #1 The Wonderful Wizard of Oz (1900) READ November 26, 2013 - December 1, 2013 
 My Kid - At first I thought it was crazy, but then it started getting awesome. I remember the movie, but there's a lot of parts that are different. 
 Me - I mean, classic, right? The book pretty much follows the film almost entirely with few exceptions. In hindsight after finishing the entire series, it is worth nothing that it is considerably one of the best books in the series, while many others are of questionable quality. 
 #2 The Marvelous Land of Oz (1904) READ December 1, 2013 - January 9, 2014 
 My Kid - It was scary... Jack Pumpkinhead and Tip escaped and it was really cool. 
 Me - This is one of the books Return to Oz was based from, The Gump and The Powder of Life coming into play to help Dorothy and Jack Pumpkinhead outwit Mombi. An enjoyable book, quite different than the first book but engineered beautifully with plot and characterization. Enjoyed this one. What was most engaging about this text was Ozma and Tip, and what this book says about gender and youth. I think there is a lot that can be examined about gender at birth and the fluidity of gender as a social construct, witch curse or no. 
 #3 Ozma of Oz (1907) READ January 9, 2014 - February 22, 2014 
 My Kid - The boat crashes and they have to ride in the box with the chicken... I like TikTok. They saved the Queen. 
 Me - This is the second book that Return to Oz was conceived from and a very engaging book. This one requires more understanding and construction of the Oz Universe including the transformation of several of our characters into ornaments and the outwitting of the Nome King in order to save our friends. This was one of my final favorites before the quality of the books fell, as far as I am concerned. 
 #4 Dorothy and the Wizard in Oz (1908) READ February 22, 2014 - August 12, 2014 
 My Kid - I kinda forgot this one. There was the vegetable people underground and nothing really happened? 
 Me - Yeah, this one was a bust for me. I think Baum was making some kind of satirical point lost to history... Or maybe the obvious non-referential one, but still, just seemed like the episodic nonsense that didn't have a point most of the time. Keep the beginning, I guess and then skip to the final third, and there's your story. 
 #5 The Road to Oz (1909) READ August 12, 2014 - February 22, 2015 
 My Kid - The love magnet was pretty awesome, and Dorothy meets the rainbow girl and Shaggy man... I guess I'll leave off there.

Um, this baffles me. 
 It seems that adults can't agree on the message. I think I have to lean towards the minority here. Existing solely to be used by others, and giving your love and care until you are diminished into almost nothing seems an odd, disturbing, and unhealthy idea for a children's book. It's like the tree is a mother, who just stands there and lets the boy suck up her energy. The narcissistic boy only comes to the tree when he needs something, and finally the tree almost ceases to exist after submitting itself to endless abuse, because it has forgotten that sometimes it's okay to do things for yourself. Classic martyrdom, an attitude that never fails to amaze me. In a bad way. 
 Or maybe this is a cautionary tale? You should not become like this boy etc. The boy is after all an idiot, who uses the tree as a commodity and a bottomless well. Unfortunately the tree allows itself to be used as a doormat, so the giving continues. However, I found no hint whatsoever anywhere (even after repeated readings) that this was meant to be a cautionary tale. 
 Oh well. I doubt children are going to be traumatized by this, and you can always discuss with your child while reading, but ultimately a book with a clear (not too dumbed down!) positive message that can't be misinterpreted might be a better choice. Let's celebrate relationships where both parties give something to the table. In my personal life I have seen relationships like the one of the tree and the boy, and they always end up in tears, once in a police car driving away from an abusive husband. Realizing that some actually consider this book as the ideal model of a relationship is sad and depressing. Just because you have your own hobbies and your sense of self intact, doesn't mean you don't care about others or your children. I just don't get why someone would want to become a mere shadow of themselves, and hide in corners apologizing for their existence.

So someone explain to me how you can have a dystopian society and then fail to give the reader any basic details to let us know how different the society is from our own. Leaving out that they cannot see color isn't a "mystery," it's annoying and confusing to the reader. Honestly if this was all a hologram world it would have made for a more plausible story. You can't just turn off colors in humans without greatly altering their eyes and how their eyes handle light. Seriously, it is a huge plot hole that isn't addressed and makes for a mediocre novel. The actual idea of "memories" being able to be quarantined and "given" is also not explained one lick, and that's another thing; I have no clue how Lois Lowry decided it could be done. No geneticist can get rid of feelings and memories, and certainly can't take a hardwired neural event and turn it into a commodity to be handed between people. As the old woman on the insurance company commercials says "that's not how any of this works!" 
 Weird inconsistencies in the society made it hard to immerse myself. You can't tell me that rules are incredibly important on one page and the next tell me that they let some of them slide without much issue. The supposedly totalitarian society also beats children for using the wrong word (citing "correct language" and not letting a kid exaggerate about starving for food) but is OK with kids learning to ride bikes before they're told it's allowed. It doesn't fit at all. 
 Also why is everyone so formal in the beginning? What kid calls a stuffed animal a "comfort object" with no issues. Why is the Release treated as such a shocker? I knew the minute they talked about it that it meant execution. It's nothing surprising. What is scary is that no one seems to have developed compassion on their own for those they like. Unless the pills they take dampen emotions, which is kind-of alluded to but not enough. I do not for one second believe or accept the idea that the boy they fostered would be put up for "release" with no complaint. Especially for a stupid reason of not being a sound sleeper. 
 I was also a little disturbed by the idea of "birthmothers" being completely sequestered and looked down upon by the rest of the community. Okay, let's just diss on the women who freaking gave birth to you, because they don't have to do anything for the years where they are pregnant and giving birth to healthy babies. I get that there is this vibe of downsizing a population (and I get the China allusions) but it is just really weird that on one hand people never meet their mothers but on the other they hate the women who were assigned to give birth. It's not like these ladies are hussies; they're told to go be mothers and get pregnant. For three babies straight. That's pretty horrible sounding to me. A huge sacrifice that a woman doesn't even get to decide about before being forced to have three babies, give them up on the spot, and then go do hard labor until they're too old to work. 
 I just don't find any of this society plausible. I give the benefit of the doubt that, somehow, there was a way to control the weather. So then apparently "other things" needed to be sacrificed too, but there is no explanation of how that is. Jonas was with the Giver for a year, and this was a short book that could have easily taken the time to explain some of the far-fetched aspects of society more. What kind of pills do they make those who have hit puberty take? Is it a sterilization pill or does it do something to suppress emotions? Why can memories be transferred between people by touch? Why does Jonas have to have his tunic off but the baby an wear clothes for this? How does the Giver know who his daughter is? (how does he ave a daughter?) Do men get selected for breeding? Is it all from the same DNA? 
 Overall too many questions and left on a useless cliffhanger that didn't need to be there ruin this book and make it feel like a lame attempt to copy 1984. 
 Also final edit: Gabe can't be Jonas' brother. It clearly states that the birthmothers have 3 babies in 3 years. So him being one means that it has to be a different mother. Unless the color of the eyes dictates a Giver/Receiver, which would mean that the Giver must have kids and that Jonas might be his kid. But whatever I'm over this book and need to stop adding things that irritate me about it to the review. I simply cannot believe some teachers use this book in school. The Anthem, Animal Farm, and 1984 are much better books to go over the same general topic.
"Comic Tragedies", Louisa May Alcott, sounds promising, right? Sadly, I can't picture any of these actually working. I wonder if these would have gone over better some hundred years ago...

 I first read this when I was young and never liked it. I found the morality in the story black-and-white and one-sided. 
 Here were the chief issues I had with it: 
 1. The villains in this story never had any chance of winning against the protagonist. There's no sense of threat. The text explicitly states that the protagonist has the upper hand because mongooses are a natural predator of snakes. If I want to get excited about a story, I need to believe that there's a credible chance the protagonist might fail, or might only win at great personal cost. By the story's climax, he all but has the main antagonist cornered and beaten. 
 2. The morality in this story is...bizarre, to say the least. There's some weird animal-racism going on in here. The protagonist has no problem with destroying an entire brood of cobra eggs without giving the hatchlings a chance to be better cobras than their parents. He doesn't distinguish them from the adult cobras, who have a sense of right and wrong but choose to do murderous things. It's like all cobras are inherently bad, just because they're cobras. 
 Adding to that, the interests of all the animals are treated as subservient to those of the humans, even though the animals are supposedly equally as sentient as them. 
 The last thing is mostly just that I identified and sympathized more with the villains of this story than the "good" characters. You could easily see this as a story about two snakes employing desperate tactics to prevent the displacement of both themselves and their family. And if you buy into the interpretation that the cobras = native Indians and the humans = imperialistic Europeans then...well.

Caveat: I am way outside the age of the target group and I read this book in the English translation.

 The language is (maybe due to the translation) very weak, the characters and their interactions unconvincing, the plot has been done many times before and for me there is nothing here to make me care about what happens; looking at the four titles of the French originals, it's going to be stereotypes galore in the future anyway.

I do not want to be unfair. This is a book for children. I am not a child, but a grumpy old man. Still, I occasionally read (and very much enjoy) YA novels, I just love funny novels and this is among the bestselling comedy books in the UK these are three valid reasons for curiosity - and there may be other adults like me tempted to try David Walliams. 
 Don't. 
 Maybe I would have fared better, if I liked his TV writing (Little Britain), but I am not a fan of that show at all, finding it either mean spirited, exploiting the worst stereotypes or just plain stupid. Sorry. 
 Gangsta Granny suffers from the same problems: It uses the lowest common denominators to gain as wide an audience as possible that it overshoots at those who actually prefer to think for themselves and ask questions. Case in point: Ben's parents are such unlikely caricatures of adults in their obsession with (and reduction to) ballroom dancing, it is painful. And though his grandmother's secret past as a thief might be a funny idea in itself (just not very original), her other persona of 'granny' is such a stereotype it should not have made it past the first editor. 
 To call David Walliams a modern Roald Dahl is very inappropriate.

The Baudelaire orphans were once again sent to live with another distant relative, Uncle Monty. Uncle Monty is a herpetologist. He studies snakes, keeps them, and takes care of them inside the Reptile Room, hence the title. Unlike Count Olaf, Uncle Monty is a good person. He is nice, he takes care of the orphans, he treats them as his own children, he gives them separate, comfortable rooms, and he lets them do what they are passionate about (Violet inventing, Klaus reading and researching, and Sunny biting things). It looked like everything's finally going well with the children's lives, until we see Count Olaf arriving at their doorstep. He's disguised himself as Stephano, Uncle Monty's new assistant. I can't explain how utterly displeased I am about Olaf's reappearance. I can't deny that I hoped for a little bit that Olaf would be no more and that there would be a different antagonist instead (since we all know that the mishaps would never cease, at least get rid of Olaf). 
 As if Olaf's arrival wasn't enough, there goes the infuriating Snicket again. Like what I said in my review for the previous book, he keeps on emphasizing the Baudelaire children's tragic, unfortunate lives. There goes a fresh, happy scene, then he ruins it by freaking spoiling us about Uncle Monty's death? Seriously, Snicket? You that desperate to make your book seem so tragic and disturbing? Nuh-uh not a clever one. Ain't cool. We clearly, absolutely, get what you're trying to say. Can you just stop? 
 I know, I shouldn't take this too complicatedly because this is a children's book. But I've read a lot of children's books, even at this age, and I enjoyed most of it a lot. Why not for this series? 
 Lemony Snicket tries so hard to be so clever it's becoming a hell lot frustrating. 
 DNF. 5 stars for Uncle Monty, but I have to give the book a 1.

I bought this book because animal fantasy is one of my favorite genres (especially when it involves rodents, and then especially when those rodents are squirrels). However, it turned out to be a complete disappointment. It is outrageous how much Britain's gray squirrels are vilified in the media, and this book is no exception. From what I've heard, it all mainly comes from propaganda spread by people who have monetary interest in killing these innocent animals. The real reason for the red squirrels' decline is habitat loss from human activity (in-depth information can be found at these websites: http://www.grey-squirrel.org.uk/ and http://www.i-csrs.com/). I was surprised that such a book could come from as good an author as Jane Yolen, and it is alarming that a story aimed at impressionable children could be so consistently negative toward a species of animal. The supposed facts - actually falsehoods - throughout will do nothing but mislead them and cause gray squirrels to be the objects of undeserved hatred. It would have been much better if Nutley had learned that they are not so bad after all. A possible friendship between he and the gray squirrel Groundling is promising at first but is never allowed to develop. Nutley's view of the grays does not change; the reader is left with the conclusion that all of them are irredeemably evil. Ultimately, no matter their part in driving the red squirrel from Britain, they are certainly not doing anything out of malice; in reality, they aren't directly attacking the reds and in some cases have lived peacefully alongside them for years. Grays and reds have at times actually shared dreys! I know this book is fictionalized, but even with anthropomorphized animals, there should be some basis in truth and a positive message for children. You won't find that here. Instead, I recommend you pick up Cyril's Woodland Quest, a story about red and grey squirrels that addresses the folly of prejudices.

** spoiler alert ** 
 So, I read this to my daughter. Storywise, it was flat, but it's only a thin book, so maybe that passes for acceptable these days - the only thing the story had was a weak twist 6-year old could see coming. The set up for this is a contrivance that has Oliver being jinxed with bad luck.... only, after the denouement, we see that this was actually good luck. So where's the continuity? 
 But there was this one part that drops this book from a 2 to a 1-star. The bully (he's even called Bully). Yes, i appreciate it was for drama, but really..... it just makes me think this author found her weak characters, and people bought the books, so she stuck to the formula to crank out a few more for the cash. 
 Anyway, back to the drama.... Bully gets one of these dangerous creatures they are warned not to touch, and puts it down Oliver's neck. The teacher goes huh? Bully says "it was an accident," and that's it. Nothing more. 
 We see this time and again in weak fiction (and not so weak, as it happens), such behaviour is accepted as the norm. It's all right to use nasty bullying to forward the plot, because it happens. 
 Well, no. This is as bad as condoning it. Oliver and friend accept what happened and believe it's for them to sort out - because adults can't or won't. 
 This is why bullying persists, folks. Because the rest of us shrug and accept that it is going to happen. Well screw you, Ms Mongredien. I'm fed up of this attitude, which does seem to permeate society, being tacitly supported by such plot contrivances. 
 Good fiction can teach so much. But bad fiction simply annoys.

This fabulously illustrated book tells the story of the most colorful fish in the sea. All of the other fish want to be just like him, but he doesn't want to share his uniqueness with them. He's afraid that if he gives away what makes him happy, he will no longer fell special or happy. 
 After reading other reviews, it is difficult to decide what meaning to take from the tale. Is he giving away everything special about him and becoming like everyone else (the socialist political view), or is this a story about the value of sharing what makes you special with others so they can be happy too? 
 Although I would like to lean toward the sharing view, I can definitely see the other side and even with the sharing view...is it right to give you wealth away to others? 
 In this case, yes. I believe it is. The fish didn't necessarily earn his uniqueness, he was born with it. There is nothing wrong with being special or different from everyone else, but if you can share what makes you special with others than you are more special because you have made other people (or fish) happy too. 
 As a children's story, I believe was Pfister is trying to get at is that kids should share their toys with their friends when they play. This doesn't mean they should give away their new shiny hat. Maybe their parents worked really hard to purchase that hat just for them and it was their only present. 
 Hmm...this is a tough one. I think I'll just leave it at that.

Almost every tale begins with "once upon a time," ends with good triumphing (and bad repenting), and contains some element of magic. My two favorite quotes from the entire collection come from "The Old Woman in the Wood" and The Iron Stone - "for he was a King's son" (400) and "in the days when wishing was having" (407), respectively - because they pretty much sum up every story. 
 This is a great thumb-through in terms of academic research, but I don't recommend reading the collection page-to-page.

It is always a dicey affair to criticise a popular book: and when it is an acknowledged classic for children, it is even more dangerous. So I agonised a lot over my impressions of Pinocchio: Is it only a matter of personal taste? Am I missing something? Should I rethink my rating based on learned opinions spanning more than a century? In the end, I decided to go with my original evaluation. 
 This is one of those stories you read and love in comics format or abridged versions before you come into contact with the original. What usually happens is that, those adaptations modify and trim the original tale to suit the sensibilities of the current generation. I also read Pinocchio as a comic book and loved it; however, on reading the original, I find that many of the "creepier" elements had been edited out of that version. 
 I do not love moral fables for children. The type of story where, for example, the disobedient little lamb is gobbled up by the big, bad wolf, crying with his last breath: "Oh! If I had only listened to my mother!" is terrifying to kids (I speak from personal experience). They are equivalent to the posters of hell which some people were fond of hanging in their drawing rooms during my childhood. In the nineteenth century, when Collodi wrote his story, one can easily understand that this must have been an accepted method of keeping children in line: by frightening them out of their wits. I do not think the modern world will look kindly on that method. 
 It is not that creepiness by itself is bad. Many fairy tales are frightening, with their suggestions of cannibalism, patricide, incest, torture etc. The difference between the fairy tale and the moral fable is that the fairy tale is a live entity, growing, shrinking and changing shape while travelling from mouth to mouth; the messages are subliminal, interacting with the child's subconscious. The moral fable on the other hand, is "purposeful" - there is a message ("if you do this, then this will happen!") which the author wants to drum into the child's head, usually by using fear as a tool. It is the narrative equivalent of the schoolmaster's swishing cane. 
 Collodi's story, taken by itself, has many wonderful elements of dark fantasy (the huge Dogfish which swallows ships whole, the snake with a tail which smokes like a chimney, the little white man who converts boys to donkeys and sells them...) and could have made a wonderful fairy tale. However, the moralising on almost every page of what happens to bad boys who do not obey their parents, do not study and tell lies takes all the fun out of it: the voice of the narrator, coming out through various parental figures, becomes sickening. What crowned the whole thing for me was the death of poor Candlewick, Pinocchio's friend, after short life of back-breaking labour as a donkey. Yuck! . I was happy when the story ended. 
 I would recommend reading it to children with the morality edited out: but why bother? There are better books out there. Or let them read it as a comic book, or watch the Disney movie.

In fact, I felt so frustrated with where this book was going (nowhere) that I put it down for a few days before trying to finish what a 24 page book! And neither the title or final words offered me any comfort when I finally finished it. My time could've been better spent curled up with A Birthday for Bear, a far more superior book the marketing people used in comparison to promote this wannabe.

I read this with my 8-year-old and we both had a difficult time liking Isabella. The story concept was very confusing and we kept hoping to have an explanation nearby (either a panel on the page or on the following page to explain the characters Isabella were portraying). 
 It wasn't obvious to us right away that the characters started their day in a hotel room in Washington, D.C. Likely, this is a technique for this series -- to lead the readers on until we get to the factual explanation page at the end -- but I think the author is missing an opportunity to educate us much earlier in the story. This is a concept that requires a lot of set up before diving into and it might even have benefited from having a lot of the factual stuff up front. 
 As for the art... we were not enchanted by Mike Litwin's pictures.

I was very much looking forward to introducing my children to the myths I grew up with and so excited to The Story of Antigone as it is part of a new series. What a boring disappointment! Ali Smith's use of having the story shared through the eyes of a crow took away from the story and did not add great value. While I admired the art from Laura Paoletti, I felt the 1st chapter (all about the crow's point of view), could've easily been edited out. Then, as I read on, I felt the dialogue between characters was very stiff and inexperienced. It lacked a flow and naturalness, and much of it also did not provide any additional value. 
 There are more exciting collections focusing on Greek stories. Please seek those out.

I was excited to read this book because I know Half Moon Bay, so even a fictionalized version made me think I was in for some fun. But the writing of this story did not work for me. The cliched characters were such an insult to their own stereotypes (do we really need another absent minded professor mad scientist uncle?) and the kids this is geared to deserve something more smartly written. The book is a great concept, however, and I hope it inspires some kids. If families take the time to build and enjoy the robots, then this book has brought some magic into people's lives. However brilliant the concept is of story + DIY science, it won't work without better written and more addictive stories. On a positive note, I liked the illustrations.

A disappointing read! i could not understand why this book is a classic and so popular.Peter is exceedingly annoying and wendy decidedly weird and submissive..i do not know any preteen girls who wish to play at being mothers to a group of boys..this book really reinforces stereotypes and i would certainly not recommend it for kids i know..this book seems to play out a weird fantasy or the author's misogynistic tendencies. So there is peter who is self absorbed, commitment phobic, and irresponsible..there is a preteen wendy who wishes to marry him and is playing at being the ideal mother and wife..and there are tinker bell and tiger lily who wish to marry peter too..like the sole aim of all these amazing women is to like a creepy, insolent peter pan who is the confident hero with a sad past..this book gives me the creeps and should be on the 'To be avoided list' esp for young girls..i wish there were stronger role models in children's literature. 
 On a side note, Captain hook is interesting!

Even as a kid, I never understood the fascination with this book. I didn't like the story or the drawings. When I got older and worked in a bookstore, the owner (who was studying children's lit) explained to me about how the pictures and the length of writing on each page built up the story to rush toward the climax. While I can appreciate it as a well-done work, I still don't like it. That horrible version of a movie recently doesn't help either.
Charlie, of course, loved it. But I just can't get into this mouse & his motorcycle. Nowhere near as good as the Ramona books.

If you're going to divide the world into two camps, then I think people who love this book and people who hate it is as good a category as any other. I'm in the latter, I'm afraid. Hate is a bit strong, I suppose, and it pains me to give Shel Silverstein only one star. I can appreciate that it's well written, and I'm normally a huge fan of Shel Silverstein's, but I find this book depressing. Sure, unconditional love is wonderful and something all parents can relate to, but the boy's selfishness ruins it for me.

I give it 1/5,it is not horror which is what it is supposed to be.I didn't like the more than one ending and you could guess everything that's gonna happen ! It is meaninglesslike I finished it in less than 10 mins I swear! well the good thing about it is that your a character in the story but I didn't like it that much.Don't recommend it

How did I miss this book my entire life? I always thought it was for the very young, but I saw it at the library by chance and realized it was a book for older readers. So I checked it out, and read it today. How dismayed I was to find it a struggle to plow through. And yes, yes, I get it, it's an allegory about grown-ups and it is a children's book but if I was a child I would have been bored and sort of creeped out. I felt very bad about this, since this is a classic that everyone adores, so how relieved I was to see 9000 one star reviews and discover that I was not alone in failing to be enchanted.
I didn't like this one. I didn't see the point. everybody was polite to each other is the only good comment I have. I will have to read through the other reviews to see what I missed.

So apparently this was the very first Suess book. Published nearly 80 years ago it is a classic indeed. I had never heard of this book before. My stepdaughter was cleaning out her room at her mother's house and brought my son a giraffe that she was given at Easter. Apparently, that giraffe had to do with this book so my son wanted me to read the book to him. 
 Normally, right here I would give a synopsis of the book but there is a more pressing issue I have to get into. So the copy I read to my son was an old one. As in it was as it was originally written. I wish I had known that there was a not so minor change made back in the late 1970s. I had sat down and was reading the book to my son while my husband sat across from us playing a game on his iPad. All the sudden I came to a part in the book that I read and after I read it I hesitated for a half a second before quickly moving along. 
 You see I came to something that shows the blatant racism you would find in the 1930s. I had just read the word "chinaman" to my son. I was horrified and couldn't even look at the corner of the page where I just knew there was going to be a horrible caricature that I did NOT want him looking at. I quickly showed him the man with a long beard in the middle of the page praying he had not looked at the picture on the left-hand side. 
 Suess had agreed to change the wording to "Chinese man" and the drawing was changed to be less stereotypical. I still haven't looked at that picture but I know that the man was yellow in color. My husband and I discussed it afterward. We both were kind of not sure how to handle the situation. Do I have a discussion with my son? Do I just let it go and hope he didn't absorb any of it? 
 In the end, we decided to let it go as my son is special needs and right now this is a discussion that he does not have the capability to understand. But we have put it on our list of future discussions to have with him. 
 As far as rating this book it was an OK book up until that point. I just can't reconcile what I read. There is also a bit in there which ticked off my inner feminist but nowhere near as much as that racist moment. I understand that at the time it was considered perfectly normal but I'm a modern person and I can't just ignore something like that. I won't ignore something like that. 
 So I'm sorry but this Suess book is a 0 out of 5 stars for me.
I wasn't a huge fan of this book. I found the illustrations strange and the story was difficult to follow.

This book is so strange. I'm not sure if it is the translation that is off or if the book is just strange. The only redeeming things about the book was the pretty images, but even those were a bit strange. 
 Thanks to Net Galley for providing me with a copy of this book and letting me write this honest review.

I've been giving a lot of low ratings to free Kindle picture books lately. I just want to clarify somewhere (I'm choosing here) that these ratings are based on the writing and not on the illustrations. I've seen several awesome artwork in children's books lately.

It doesn't say anywhere that this is a retelling of a Hans Christian Anderson story. And the message seems pretty anti-diveristy if you put it into today's context. It's not a bad story, just boring and not current.

I read this as a bedtime story to my 6 yr old son. He liked it. I like Richler's extensive vocabulary, many times we stopped to discuss the meanings of words. It is a satire, but not a mean one. Richler's ongoing fascination with the workings of the law can be a bit much for younger readers, rather dry and not sure how much meaning comes through. The characters are unforgettable, lots of fun to be had there. The clairvoyant's gamble is great fun. I absolutely hated the mirror writing, when I was trying to get through a bedtime chapter at the end of a long day the last thing. I wanted to do was read backwards mirror writing. It might have been more fun for a young reader on his own. Not as much fun as The Hooded Fang, but a good time nonetheless.

Unfortunately, although this picture book appealed to my twisted sense of humour, my kid found it extremely upsetting. The only way to ease his distress was to promise him I would post his review here. Cute bunny made evil by overwriting, not fun for the kindergarten sensibilities, alas.

This story takes place after Charlie and The Chocolate Factory ends. It begins with Charlie, his grandpa, and Willie Wonka in the Great Glass Elevator. They fly over to Charlie's house and pick up the rest of the family and from there events start to happen. They accidentally end up in space. They have a run in with other astronauts, a conversation with the president, and a battle with an insect/animal thingy from another planet. They eventually make their way back to the factory where even more events ensue, namely with the grandparents. This book was odd and unusual which made it somewhat interesting, but for me it wasn't enough. There was a lot of adult humor. It's not bad, but didn't really hold my interest. The author Dahl is one of the most creative writers I've read for children's books, but even with that in mind, this book is only mediocre.

To be fair, I don't really know if this is good or not. All my abandoned books get one star because if I can't even make it through 5 pages in a week (this book) and I start reading something else, I didn't like it.
I wanted to like it, really ... but the story went nowhere.

Sweet mother of Christ, how did I ever manage to read this book in the seventh grade? Talk about grimdark and violent, man. I appreciate some of the ideas and themes in the book, but it is far too plagued with gory throat-ripping, xenophobia, and sexism to really enjoy or want to think too intently on this piece.

This story does not match the pretty art at all. This is an extremely ugly story about a grandmother yelling at Bella about trees. and I think there is some sort of language differences, as the word choice is really strange for me. Pick another Christmas book.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I only put this book on my children's book bookshelf based on the most general of definitions. This cheery, little picture book follows a little fish named Arlene's transition into a sardine. I DO NOT recommend reading this book to children, especially the young and impressionable. This opinion would carry over to any book in which the main character dies less than halfway through and is then processed into food.
I appreciate this for its place in children's literary history, but man is this not a good book. Peter is mean and violent and the whole plot is disturbing -- with a healthy dose of sexism thrown in.

Just kind of a super strange way of dealing with pet death (I know that some kids wouldn't have been devastated by the death of a pet fish, but replacing fish after fish without eliciting any emotion from the child? The blatant and continued lying from the mom?). Pass.

I received a complimentary copy from NetGalley in exchange for my honest review. 
 Ummm . . . what? From the elaborate summary, I assumed that this would be a chapter book, but it is a picture book (with very few words). Which is fine, I suppose, and the illustrations are intriguing (though somewhat ghoulish), but there exists little to no understandable plot. The last page came and I had absolutely NO idea what I had just read.

I may love Chris Colfer in his acting career, but I will say again that just because you have the money and/or fame to get a work published does NOT mean that you deserve that honor. The Wishing Spell is unoriginal and unsuitable even for a very basic level of YA audience. Give your fantasy-loving friends something like Jasper Fforde's Thursday Next series (adult audience) or Gail Carson Levine's absolute classic Ella Enchanted (YA and adult appropriate) if they are looking for a plot that plays successfully with the conventions of fairy tale narrative. Skip this novel -- one that, if anything, is carried entirely on Colfer's Glee fame . . . you deserve better.

To be honest, I would have never picked up this book if I wasn't reading it for a class. It was so cliche-ridden and laughably idiotic, I had a hard time getting through it. On top of that, I thought this was a book about a nurse, not a detective. If I had wanted a story about a female amateur detective, I would have picked up a Nancy Drew book. I will admit, though, that the mystery did make this book less unbearable. I was just nearly pulling my hair out because the clues were so obvious and the characters so clueless, pun absolutely intended. Not to mention I thought it was pathetic that Cherry's patients were "asthmatics". It made them sound like having asthma was like having a terminal illness. It was ridiculous from cover to cover. And Cherry--I have a hard time taking her seriously just by her name--was absolutely ridiculous. She had no flaws whatsoever, except for the fact that she was prone to tears whenever somebody threw the littlest comment her way, and for her tendency to get herself into dangerous situations (Torry Torrington pointed that out as one of her flaws. That's right--Torry Torrington. Does anybody else find the name incredibly funny?). Okay, I'll stop now. 
 SENSITIVITY WARNING: Uuuhhh, other than being absolutely ridiculous? It might have unintended sexist or racist remarks that were typical of the fifties. Other than that, clean as a slate (in plot as well as profanities). 
 Sorry, I'll stop the bashing now.

I love Roald Dahl. A number of his books reside in my permanent favorites list (The BFG, Matilda, etc), but this was just a loosely cobbled together nonsense. The story had no purpose. Some of the caricatures served their satirical purpose well, but there was no holistic sense to the book. Also, Dahl contradicts the physical world too much and not in a way that seems to serve any narrative purpose. I was surprised how exceedingly messy this book was.

It's been quite a while since I read this book so I can't really say much about it. I didn't really like it when I read it, though. The main reason why I didn't really like the book much was because I didn't get why the characters had to be mice. This won't seem like a big deal to most people but it seemed to me that the characters could have been humans and everything else would have stayed exactly the same. Well, almost everything else. At one point I decided that the characters could just be humans and imagined them as humans. Then, somewhere else, the author described a scene that involved a character's tail, which was weird. Yes, I understand it was wrong of me to imagine them as people even though the author said they were mice but the thing is he did almost nothing to make it seem as if the society was at least somewhat different than a human society. At least in the movie Antz, the ants don't fly airplanes and make watches. They tunnel through the ground and instead of drinking beer like humans, they drink something out of other bugs. There was no reason for the characters in the book to be mice. It's kind of the same reason why I didn't like the graphic novel "Maus." And I didn't find the story to be that exciting. However, it's just a matter of taste and I'm pretty sure that kids in 5th grade (that was when I read the book) would like the book.

Pretty good book. Nice, heart-touching story. 
 EDIT: 
 Oh wait, I change my mind. This book sucks. I previously gave it four stars. That was because I was remembering it with the mind of a teenager looking back at it with nostalgia. But I suddenly remembered how I felt about the book when I was in first grade and my teachers (we had two) read it to us and when I read it myself a few years later. I was more logical back then and hated books with talking animals because animals can't talk. 
 Anyway, because I was more logical back then, I thought about things that I probably wouldn't care about if I read it now. 
 Why should we care about the pig? All the other animals were going to get killed someday. Why should we care just for the pig? 
 Why did people think that the pig was special just for STANDING UNDER A WEB? I remember thinking that that was incredibly stupid. I wouldn't have paid any attention to the pig. Anyone with a quarter of a brain cell would know that the spider was special and not the pig. 
 I do remember feeling very sad at the beginning when the girl stops her father from killing the pig and at the end (if you've read the book, you can probably guess why). But I remember those parts being so...what's a good word? Mawkish. Yes, let's go with that. 
 I'm not saying E.B. White's a bad writer. Of course I'm not. TRUMPET OF THE SWAN is still one of my favorite books that were written for children. But this book sucks (in my opinion).

** spoiler alert ** 
 I read this book a pretty long time ago as well as Charlie and the Chocolate Factory. Back then, I disliked both. Back then, I would have given the former and the latter only 1 star each. However, I really like Charlie and the Chocolate Factory now. Now I would give CCF 5 stars. My opinion of Danny the Champion of the World hasn't changed, though. Sure the villain is mean and I kind of wanted something bad to happen to him. The problem is that it's Danny and his father and some other people in their town who just gang up on him and steal his pheasants and whatnot. They don't steal because they have to to survive, either. They steal just for the fun of it. So, unlike CCF, this book doesn't give a very good message. But it's not really the moral I look for, it's the story. And the story just wasn't as fun as CCF.

It's a great blurb.....I read it to my son and found the story rambling and fairly non-sensical....but not in a good way. I'm afraid I was very glad to finish. the whole pretext of the tree and Toby's family doesn't work. It's so spread out that you basically forget who on earth you are reading about now.

If your patrons love Pokemon, then this is a good easy reader for them, even though purchasing it will make librarians cringe. One day, Ash, Brock, and Misty meet an old man named Old Man Shuckle. He creates a rare juice that makes Pokemon easier to train and catch after they drink it. He sends our heroes out to catch a rare blue Shuckle so he can get the juice out of its shell. However, Team Rocket catches first! Jessie drinks the juice, and all of the Pokemon fall in love with her. 
 The text is white and large, which make it easy to read against the full color pages. The illustrations are the biggest disappointment. It is clear that they are just images from the television series that are just printed for this easy reader. They depict the actions that the characters do, which can be helpful. While professionals will dislike this book for it's lack of character development and cheating with by using screen shots from the television show, younger readers will like it for those same reasons. The characters are familiar, and the text is very easy to read. This is recommended as an additional purchase for readers ages 5 to 7. However, if your patrons are demanding more Pokemon tomes, then this would be a recommended purchase.
Instant classic? I think not. The only thing that this book has going for it are the illustrations. Hence the single star.

Gingerbread Friends is the story of the Gingerbread Baby and his search for friends. He lives in Mattie's room, but Mattie doesn't always want to play with him, so the Gingerbread Baby decides to go into town to find his own playmates. The only problem is, no one wants to play with him. The only thing I liked about this book was the recipe for gingerbread. 
 Genre: picture book 
 Copyright: 2008

The only thing I enjoyed about this book was the pictures. I'm not really sure why it has won awards since there are much better picture books out there. If I was a child, I would be bored by the story, but I guess it might be nice to read since it's a bit predictable. 
 Copyright: 2008 
 Genre: picture book

Poor Puppy is an alphabet book for children. The puppy's best friend is the kitty, but unfortunately the kitty doesn't want to play with the puppy. So, he takes a nap instead and dreams of all the games they will play. 
 Genre: picture book 
 Copyright: 2007
It was ok. I enjoy her 43 Old Cemetery Road series much more.
For some reason this one just didn't appeal to me. It isn't much different than many others and I know to expect the prejudice of the time period, etc.

I think the spirit the girls usually show in these books is missing in this one. I understand, of course, they would be depressed and worried because their friends and family members have gone off to war but it seems to linger throughout the book and they don't seem to have a lot of the effort to make the best of a bad situation and carry on, which they usually do in these types of books. Even the kidnapping of the twins seems more like just another reason for the characters, particularly Mollie who isn't as close to the men who are in the war, to have something to be depressed about.
absolutely hated it and had to read it twice for school

this book gave me nightmares 
 I am not exaggerating

I thought I would like this book more than I actually did. I know the book is written in journal format and that is fine but who would have thought a mundane book would have been a Newberry award winner?

DNF. Poorly pitched agewise, plot inconsistencies, overly clever punny names pointed out far too many times in case the reader is not smart enough to have gotten them (we are), stereotypical and flat characters that seem to have come out of an Enid Blyton novel. 
 Full review @booklikes

I had high expectations for this book as this is one that is considered a classic Australian children's book. Unfortunately, this counts as one of my least favourite books of all time. I enjoyed nothing about this book or my experience reading it and despite the short-length, it was a struggle to finish. I was familiar with the general story, having seen the film based on this book many times. I found the film to be quite average, and my feeling was the story would likely work better with younger characters as the film's characters were around 15 while the book characters were about 11-12. Despite this, the book did not work at all for me. I felt that while the behaviour made more sense with this age cohort, it actually failed to make the characters any more relatable. Everything in this book was annoying. I hated every single character in this book and I was not interested in the plot whatsoever. The problem is with this book is that the story itself actually has no plot. It seems like a series of semi-related events with nothing happening or anything to tie these events together adequately. In my opinion, if you are interested in the story, I would watch the movie as I got much more enjoyment from that than reading this book.

If I had read this after I read the first book when I was a kid I'm sure that I would have enjoyed it immensely but, I read it as an adult so I didn't find it enjoyable at all. 
 This book picks up where the first book left off but it makes no sense at all. They go to space, fight aliens, smash through the roof of the factory, de-age the re-age the grandparents and finally get invited to the White House. The whole book is written like the nonsensical ramblings of a lunatic. While I'm glad that I read it, I did not enjoy it at all. Good thing it's only 180 pages or I would have given up on it.

I don't usually find myself unenthusiastic about a Caldecot medal book, but this story just doesn't speak to worthwhile values (at least on face value from my preliminary read). Rejecting human community for that of horses? Loving a stallion to the point that she becomes his mare? No thanks. I did find the illustrations to be a redeeming element: they are quite striking.
Guess I don't relate well to dog ownership...

I was disappointed by this book. I could maybe see it working for a one on one setting or for a child to read on their own, but there really just wasn't much there to work with. For my purposes as a librarian, it just fell flat. 
 For: fans of man's best friend; readers wanting a more basic book who are wanting to add their own context. 
 Possible red flags: various adventures and messes; not very complex.

Joey has the problem of always being high stung and he can't seem to get himself to concentrate on anything. Lately, his attention disorder has been manifesting in ways where people get hurt and Joey must now go to a special school to figure out how he can improve. Joey must learn to change his behaviors, accept his home life, and he must also become accustomed to new medication. 
 I really didn't like this book. There was just a push for the child to constantly be medicated and the abusive homelife is hardly addressed in therapy. No one takes the time to explain to Joey that he isn't being punished, so he thinks that he's a bad kid that needs to be sent away. I learned that there are other books that are attached to this one--companion books or part of a series--and it's unclear if these issues are resolved in those installments. Either way, the professionals in his life should have explained things to him and the absence of that conversation still bothers me.

To be honest, I have no idea why anyone likes this book at all. I saw the cover and thought it looked interesting. Should have thought, never judge a book by its cover, but I didn't. That night, I sat in bed and read the first few chapters before saying, "this is the worst book I have literally ever read" and set it down. I decided to finish because I am not one to quit and had to force myself to stay awake as I stumbled aimlessly into the abyss of random words. The writing is bad, the story is stupid, and unless you are four or under, this is the most boring book in the world!!!!

This book was one of the worst pieces of writing I have ever read. The short but uninteresting plot will leave readers wondering why they have wasted two hours of their life wondering when the book would end? The book has a terrible plot and the characters are just two little brats who get lost in a museum while running away. It was a horrible book. It had no good message to kids besides the fact that running away is not a good idea. Otherwise, do not read this book. Or anything that has a Newbury award. They are always the worst!

First off, I just want to say that this book was only read because it was my Lois Lowry. This book is about the stupidest book i have ever read. The children get abandoned by their parents and have a baby show up at their doorstep. Lowry tries to put comedy into this weird story but it ends up backfiring. Ex. She named the two twins Timothy A and Timothy B, but you just get confused when reading and aren't able to develop feelings for one because you don't know if he is the right one. Terrible book and appalling for someone like Lois Lowry to sink so low.
a silly story line, and basically about a Bear who steals food. not worth the effort of even getting the book from the library.
there is enough coarseness and disrespect in the world without adding to it by reading this book aloud to a child.
a stupid premise for a book...unless you eat all your candy, then no vegetables (spinach).
This story about a garbage truck and its daily life is tedious, not much fun to read aloud.
I did not care for this story at all...starts about being factual (about a girl who is afraid to try anything new, and then turns into a somewhat dark fantasy, and ends in a ridiculous fashion

This is the first book of the Harry Potter series I've read. I watched the first two movies, though, and started with this book because I was told it is the best of the seven. 
 The story was good, and I didn't get very bored, but that was about it. I read it so fast that I can't complain about the time it took, but I don't understand the people who say that this childrens' book should also be read by adults. I suppose that, in a way -- if you just want a mindless read to help you relax -- this could be a good choice, but otherwise I can't really recommend it. It's best quality is that it manages to avoid the pitfalls of simply telling a story, for example dwelling on a point simply to build suspense or adding complexity for its' own sake, but doesn't add anything new to the genre. In the end, it's still a kids' book. 
 Almost immediately upon finishing this book, I moved on to The Picture of Dorian Gray, and within five pages felt somehow more alive, even though it'll probably take me about as long to read 200 of Wilde's pages as it did to read 450 pages of Rowling's.

I read this book when I was ten or eleven. At one point, I threw it across the room and burst into tears( I then had to climb down from my bunk-bed, get the book, and climb back up, so I could finish it)! It was the first book that made me cry.
This book scarred me for goddamned life. I still can't get rid of a stuffed animal. Do you have any idea how many stuffed animals live in my basement because of this book?
I hate this book. I will never ever go to Alaska because I don't want to cut off my own feet and join a dog-sled race.
If I were younger, the age the book is meant for, I might have enjoyed it. Who knows? Not a book that crosses age groups.

I really wanted to like this book. I love Chris Colfer as an actor and as a person, but unfortunately I can't love him as an author. This book felt like he took the general idea from The 10th Kingdom, injected it with some plot points from Once Upon A Time, threw some Narnia on it and then wrote a bad fanfic about it. The book has a few nice moments (especially at the end), but those don't excuse the many bad parts. It is stated many times that the two main characters had an epic adventure that seemed impossible at the start while in fact everything was resolved without much effort and they didn't really have any character development. Everything felt dumbed down, predictable and there were a lot of errors and plotholes. 1 star. 
 I heard Chris already finished book 2. I hope his writing has improved, but I won't spend any more money to find out.

While the illustrations were lovely and I liked the initial tale - the quest for the feather to find his owner. However, as the story progressed I found myself liking it less and less. When the hawk attacked the only nice bird in the bunch it was disturbing. Immediately after that scene, the bird lands and a chicken find him and puts him in her wing. It was an abrupt ending and unsatisfying as well. 
 I received a copy of this book for free in exchange for my review. All opinions are my own.

Somebody got me this book when I was 9 or 10. At that point, it was always a good bet that you could buy me anything with a horse in it and I would be happy. Except that in this particular book, the horse dies. Horribly. Riddled with arrows. Sorry to give away a major plot point, but it scarred me. The book was banished, but it haunts me to this day.
Highly disturbing tale about murderous cats. Me-oww indeed!

This book is a 150-page PSA for library cards... and frankly, the TV series "Arthur" did that much better in a half-hour musical. ("Having fun isn't hard / When you've got a library card!") You'd be hard-pressed to find a bigger proponent of library cards than myself, but this has all the subtlety of a sledgehammer. Apparently, having a library card cures all ills: wanting to drop out of school, missing a parent, and TV addiction (which, in the book's worst hyperbole, apparently annhilates your life if you turn on the TV... as contrasted to the perfectly healthy behavior of running up to strangers and proclaiming your favorite color). Any kid who can actually power through this book - I got about 70% in when my train arrived - likely doesn't need the moral about library cards, so this entire book is self-defeating.

I can see that the repetition in this series is going to get on my nerves more as we go on. Mr Poe drops the children at the house of a new guardian. They settle in, but then Count Olaf turns up!  It just felt like I was reading the same story for the third time - but instead of being set in a Reptile Room, it was sat in a house with a Wide Window. That drastic change is the only real alteration (well, that and their new guardian fakes her own suicide to attempt to evade Olaf's evil clutches, which I could not remember of my first reading of the book). 
 While the repetition would have given the book a lower rating anyway, there was one main aspect that pushed my exasperation at this novel into the realm of sheer frustration: I was really irritated by the language used towards one of Count Olaf's comrades. 
 "The one who looks like neither a man nor a woman," Violet replied. Klaus shuddered. "That's the scariest one." 
 I don't know why Daniel Handler - sorry, Lemony Snicket - felt the need to perpetuate gender stereotypes in a children's story, particularly when he followed up this quote by referring to the character in question as 'the creature'. 
 It's wholly inappropriate, and I know that this was written a few years ago but it's offensive and unnecessary. That's why I've only rated this installment one star: as well as recycling a plot line and using the same sentence structures throughout three books, it doesn't use language that will teach children acceptance of others. I'm the one left shuddering.

I preface this review with a note of gratitude to my dear friend who gave us this book. It was a thoughtful gift, and I will forever treasure that thought. Now, a review: 
 While the pictures are very nice, the verse, the choice of subject matter, and the presentation of that matter were infuriating. I don't know Reynolds personally, but this book leads me to believe that she is a bad person. 
 The verse is wildly uneven. We start out with your boring, but respectable, four line AABB rhyming scheme, but it only takes her until the letter D before she apparently got stuck and decided to screw it. For the rest of the book, the lines vary in length and number and sometimes she can't even be bothered to make a rhyme at all. If there was a meter, I was too angry to notice. 
 Because already by the letter E we have "explorer" which depicts a Frenchman and his little moustache paddling all by his European lonesome down the river in a native canoe. So, on the one hand, it's a word of no exclusive importance to Indiana and square on the other it whitewashes the entire concept of exploration -- which would not be half so irritating if N didn't stand for "Native." Yes, the state of Indiana, the book proudly proclaims, was named (WHICH ALSO BEGINS WITH N OMG) for Native Americans Who Were Displaced the Hell Out the State ASAP Indians an absurd term first used in the Americas by cinnamon-and-gold-obsessed Europeans with a very poor understanding of geography. 
 I is for Indianapolis, which Reynolds claims is where the laws "that make our state so great" are made. It is here that I began to suspect that Reynolds is a Republican, a liar, or has taken up residence down a well. 
 L is for Lincoln. So, apparently, is the letter Z. Let me tell you something about Indianans: they are obsessed with the notion that Lincoln lived there for like two weeks as a kid.** They will not let it go. Twenty six letters and they give TWO of them to a toddler. 
 M: ". . . fast cars race around the track / 200 times before they come back." THEY COME BACK TWO HUNDRED TIMES. 
 Q is for Quayle. A state full of glorious quarries, and Reynolds goes with Quayle. 
 R is the most insulting: actual poet James Whitcomb Riley. This would lead me to believe that Reynolds may have, at some point in her life, seen a poem, but she sure didn't bother to put any in this book. Jim, I don't know any of your poems, but I'm still sorry you had to be a part of this. 
 S, where "In olden days, schools taught the Golden Rule," because nowadays all they teach is rap music and gender studies. Is that what you are getting at, Reynolds? IS IT? 
 T is for Tulip Tree, a fine choice. It's the state tree and a beautiful one. "[T]his tree grows big, so you can play in its shade for hours," says the poem. Meanwhile, the picture shows a khaki bedecked dude and his tow headed offspring playing GOLF in the SUN. 
 It was at this point that I asked my own son if I could put the book in the trash. To my dismay, he said no. 
 V is for Vincennes. The verse touts the state's first newspaper and public library. The picture is of George Rogers Clark for some reason.* 
 X is for . . . nothing. Reynolds could find no word that begins with X. She says you can find Xs on railroad crossing signs. "Crossroads of America," she says. Fine. Trains are fine. Maybe one will roll by and put the deer in the picture out of its misery. 
 "Y is for Yellow, a mellow yellow." No. Stop. 
 My god. I've just looked and there is a real poem at the very end. Not, like, one of Riley's, but some other nerd. What is this? Penance? You think this Arthur Mapes fellow is going to repair the damage you've done to my night, Reynolds? HA. I don't even LIKE poetry! You could have spared yourself so much trouble if you'd just given up on the rhyming. You already have a thousand words of exposition crammed into the sides. Why didn't you just go with that? As it stands, I'm too wound up by the experience to even consider reading it. 
 Oh well. At least I got to do some yelling while I read it to my kid. Hooray yelling! 
 ** It's hyperbole. Don't message me. I don't care. 
 * Yes I know there are six gajillion words of prose on the sides explaining things, but I'm not going to sit here and read them all to a five year old who's skirting bedtime too closely already.

11-year old Delly is considered a bad kid by her family and teachers because of her behavior--but she doesn't really understand what is so bad about what she does. For example, if the weather is too nice to miss during the day, she simply skips school; when she sees a canoe on the river that she wants to ride in, she just takes it. Is that so wrong? She just understand doesn't why everyone calls her a bad kid...and hearing it over and over again starts to make her think she is a bad person through and through. 
 Things change when a new girl named Ferris Boyd arrives in town--she doesn't speak and won't let anyone touch her. Delly takes an immediate interest in her and decides that she wants to be her friend. She, Ferris, and Delly's younger brother R.B. end up spending a lot of time together in a tree house in the woods near Ferris's house. Being around timid Ferris and sweet R.B. help to make Delly more aware of her actions and the effects her actions have on others, and she starts to be not as much as a trouble kid as she was before. 
 I have to say that I didn't enjoy this book at all. As I listened to it, I knew that this was going to make it onto a list somewhere (themes of: 'bad kid' main character on a road to self-discovery, sibling rivalry/sibling love, making new friends/learning to get along with others, troubled friend with a troubled homelife, etc.)...but it's not that good! The first thing that struck me was Delly's ridiculous made-up vocabulary--some might find it charming, but I found it extremely irritating. I also didn't find Delly all that likable; she's bossy, acts before she thinks, and is wild. Finally, the fact that Ferris doesn't speak and the fact that animals seem to magically flock to her might appear to be related to an unsuspecting young reader. Even the ending of the book is unrealistic! I haven't read anything else by Katherine Hannigan, but I think I'll stay away from the rest of her books.

This story is told from the point of view of an angel who is hundreds of years old and living quite peacefully in a tower of a house in the Alps until a family moves in. Zola and her father are Americans who move to Switzerland to get a fresh start; her father plans to open a boarding school. The angel isn't used to people being able to see it, so it's startled when Zola addresses it when she enters the tower. 
 The angel and Zola become wary friends; Zola often asks it questions it doesn't know the answer to (are you a boy angel or a girl angel?; where are your wings?; etc.). As time passes, Zola and the angel get more used to each other. Zola begins asking the angel to help her with things; most importantly, Zola has discovered a group of orphans living in an old shed. The angel wonders what it can do to help; it seems uncertain of its role as an angel. What it can do, however, is send a sort of feeling/image into the heads of the local adults that will make them want to help the children and, alternatively, it can send feelings/images into the heads of the orphan children that will make them feel better. Will this be enough to save these children? 
 This is a gentle story that readers will be sure to remember. The angel is so innocent; it doesn't even know how to properly pronounce certain words although it's been around so long. Zola can be bossy, but her heart is in the right place. Readers who enjoyed this might also enjoy Beyond the Station Lies the Sea (Richter).

Sixth-graders Tommy, Calder, and Petra are drawn to Frank Lloyd Wright's Robie House (built in 1910) after their eccentric teacher tells their class that the house will be "murdered" and that its pieces will be sent to various museums around the world. When sharing this news, she asks the class to wonder whether or not this house is a piece of art and what the ramifications of splitting it apart would be. 
 Determined to save the house from destruction, the two boys and one girl form their own group: The Wright 3. Each member has a role throughout the story; Tommy uses his searching and digging skills to find clues, Calder uses his pentominoes (small letter-shaped tools used by mathematicians) to sort out ideas, and Petra uses the copy of The Invisible Man she finds to help guide her thoughts. One might think that saving a house from ruin would be a safe little endeavor; however, The Wright 3 find themselves in dangerous situations both on their own and as a group more than once. Someone...or something...doesn't want this house demolished! 
 The Wright 3 is a sequel to the book Chasing Vermeer, but you don't have to read that first to understand this book. And the illustrations of the house by Brett Helquist are great! The three kids risk a lot to save the Robie House...would you do the same?

Let me explain my rating here. 
 I remembered enjoying the movie as a kid, and I had never read anything from Roald Dahl before. I thought reading about the super-smart and book-loving little girl would be fun. What is was instead: frustrating. I don't know if it's because it was written in 1988 (which is not so long ago) or what but I just can't fathom how a book that presents careless, negligent parents and a teacher that endlessly insults little kids for the worse reasons and PHYSICALLY HURT them should be read to the youngs at all. 
 Like when that monster of a headmistress grabs a 5 year old kid by the hair while saying he shouldnt be alive and the kids describe it as QUOTE: a splendid entertainment. Or when her mother try to convince Matilda that you have to choose between looks or books, basically that being smart isn't useful and not something to strive for, when her father explain to his kids how much of a crook he is and how proud he is about it. Or just the way her parents completely abandon her at the end, as if to say to kids, well if you don't like your parents you should go stay with someone else. 
 I kept repeating to myself that the exageration of everything is intended, but I don't see the point in reading a story to a kid if you have to keep explaining at every turn that what the characters are saying/doing is wrong. All in all, I didn't enjoy my read as much as I expected and probably won't read any of Dahl's other stories.

 One could not but help notice the racism and sexism running through the novel.The reference to Chirag Gupta's height is certainly racist, why not name any other boy as being of lower than average height, the only reference that the book carries of Indians is in this example of Gupta, with regards to the height. Girls only like nail polish and lip gloss, this is what this book supposedly says, and I was just left wondering, if young children are indeed reading this book, then what kind of attitude would they develop not only towards the opposite sex but also towards people from other races? 
 This novel seems to be teaching children ( in an oblique way, of course ) that hurting your friends is O.K., being mean to one's best friend is O.K., belittling other s is O.K., as other people are belittling you anyway ! So, Greg is belittled and make fun of by his classmates, but I have no sympathy towards his character as he does the same to his best friend and his younger brother!So, when his best friend - Rowley is hurt, he is not bothered with the fact that well his friend is hurt, in fact he can only think of himself and how can also get the attention of girls, envying the attention Rowley gets.

 I am often torn between the idea that should Art be for Art's Sake ? And till date I don't have a clear opinion on the matter, however, when it comes to children's book, I think I have a clear one, the writers need to be responsible towards the kind of target group that they intend to wrote for, and when you are writing from the perspective of the underdog, do so. Don't just make a title in to a catchy one in order to make your book sell and please do get the meaning of ' wimpy kid ' right before writing about one.

I read this many times as a small child. Then the library moved into a new building, and they must have discarded their copy in the move, because I never saw it again. I remembered many details, but not the author's name, so I didn't realize it was the one by L. Frank Baum until a friend mentioned that book recently. 
 I read the Project Gutenberg text on my Kindle, and I think the lack of all the beautiful illustrations did away with the nostalgia I might have felt. Instead I was really underwhelmed. 
 This is probably just my problem for disliking Baum's writing. I find the things he makes up -- the character- and place-names, the world-building, the magic -- trite and just not to my taste. I don't care about the characters in this book and didn't produce any of the emotions that I was supposed to. There's a scene in which Santa Claus has become old and will soon die, and all the fairies decide to give him the one and only Mantle of Immortality so that he can continue his good work. This is clearly supposed to be a very touching episode, but I ended up just being skeptical and mildly appalled that the world contained nobody more deserving of immortality than a toy-maker. 
 The toy-making is actually the only part I really like. The idea is that Claus becomes Santa Claus because he invents toys -- he begins by whittling a model cat, and then branches out to dolls, musical instruments, etc. I liked the descriptions of how he enjoyed making things and then making children happy by giving them away. There wasn't enough of this part for me. 
 What most surprised me was how completely un-religious the story is. My memory (probably bringing in part of some other story, or making things up) had told me that the shift from Claus giving away toys at random to giving them on only one night of the year occurred at the birth of Christ, and that there was a scene in which Claus encounters the infant Jesus. This doesn't happen at all -- Christmas Eve exists ready-made and Baum never draws any connection whatsoever between the gift-giving part of Christmas and the religious feast. He even explains the "Santa" part of Santa Claus's name simply by saying that "It is possible for any man, by good deeds, to enshrine himself as a Saint in the hearts of the people." 
 I don't know that this is really wrong, but it seems like lazy storytelling to me. Or rather, that Baum used the barest idea of Santa Claus to make up a story out of whole cloth (or the sad little odds and ends in his imagination -- sorry, Oz fans!) without referring at all to the existing stories about the Saint.

 Beatrix Potter did not see a need to provide definitions for her words, and she certainly didn't pick the simplest either - but her books are classics; *children's* classics that is. And I think she had the right idea. Children don't always need explanations - they often catch on and then benefit from figuring it out on their own. Children learn how to speak and write best from books rich in vocabulary. Don't withhold them from gleaming and gaining a wealth of knowledge by writing (or reading) inferior works.

 I've been told repeatedly I'm dead wrong about that, but I read the book right when it came out just three years after The Changeling, and I keep going back and reading the book every few years and I keep seeing the same thing. Although it is well-written, it is quite clear where she got the plot. 
 Maybe I'm a bit edgy about this book because it received better marketing than The Changeling and has never been out of print. Not to mention the movie. There was an attempt by a British studio to make a film version of The Changeling in the late 1970s but it fell through. The Changeling is kind of a sleeper or cult classic, though -- people who know it are passionate about it. 
 The Changeling is good if you want a book with the same theme which makes sense and has beautiful in-depth portrayals of children creating and enacting stories in an imaginary world. If you just want a ripping good story about children who invent an imaginary world and then find themselves inside it, minus all the relevance, read The Secret Country and its sequels.
